key_terms.meaning: Software that sits between programs and hardware, managing resources and giving programs a clean, usable machine.
The OS role of deciding which program gets the CPU, memory, disk or device, and when, and for how long.
A simplified model of hardware, such as a file instead of disk sectors, so programs never touch raw devices.
A signal from a device or software that makes the CPU stop its current work and jump to OS handler code.
A table of addresses of interrupt handlers, indexed by interrupt number, so the CPU knows where to jump.
A controller moves a block of bytes between device and memory without the CPU copying each byte.
An early OS style that ran one job at a time from a prepared deck of jobs, with no user interaction during the run.
Keeping several jobs in memory so the CPU runs one while others wait for I/O, raising CPU utilisation.
Switching the CPU rapidly among many interactive users so each sees a responsive machine of their own.
A hardware mode bit marks code as kernel (privileged) or user (restricted), so user code cannot run privileged instructions.
A hardware counter that interrupts the CPU after a set interval, so the OS regains control from user code.
An instruction, such as halting the CPU or loading a page table base, that only kernel-mode code may execute.
The controlled entry point by which a user program asks the kernel to do work on its behalf.
Ready-made programs shipped with the OS (shell, compiler, file utilities) that sit on top of system calls.
A user interface that reads typed commands and runs them as system programs or system calls.
A structure where the whole OS — scheduler, file system, drivers — runs as one program in kernel mode.
A structure that keeps only the minimum (IPC, scheduling, basic memory) in kernel mode and runs services as user processes.
Separating what should be done (policy) from how it is done (mechanism), so policy can change without kernel edits.
A small program in firmware or on disk that loads the kernel image into memory and starts it.
A hypervisor runs whole guest OSes on virtual hardware; containers instead share one kernel and isolate only user space.
An array of bits where bit i records the state of block i, commonly used for free-space management.

takeaways: The OS does two jobs at once: it manages resources fairly and safely, and it hides hardware behind simple abstractions like process, file and address space.
A computer system is a CPU, memory and device controllers joined by buses; interrupts and DMA make device handling efficient and give the OS control.
Operating systems grew from batch to multiprogramming to time-sharing, and then split into real-time, mobile, distributed and cloud forms.
Dual mode plus a timer is the basic safety net: user code cannot run privileged instructions, and it cannot keep the CPU forever.

OS services split into those that help the user (interface, program execution, I/O, files, communication, error detection) and those that keep the system efficient (resource allocation, accounting, protection).
A system call is a deliberate trap into the kernel; the standard families are process control, file management, device management, information maintenance, communication and protection.
Kernel structure is a trade-off: a monolithic kernel is fast but large, a microkernel is small and reliable but pays IPC cost, and layers trade performance for clean design.
Building turns source into a kernel image; booting moves firmware to bootloader to kernel to the first user process, and policy/mechanism separation keeps design flexible.

Kernels lean on classic data structures — arrays, lists, queues, trees, hash tables, bitmaps — and the computing environment (traditional, mobile, cloud, container, real-time, distributed) decides what the OS must optimise.
bank_note: Long answers here usually mix three threads — the resource-manager/abstraction view of the OS, the hardware mechanisms (interrupts, dual mode, timer, DMA) that make protection possible, and the software structures (services, system calls, kernel structures, boot) — so expect questions that ask you to connect hardware protection to OS services rather than recite either alone.

bank.q: Explain the two roles of an operating system — resource manager and abstraction layer — using a single example of a program reading a file from disk.
outline: Names the resources: CPU time, main memory, disk blocks, device access
Shows the abstraction: open/read/write on a named file, not sectors and tracks
Shows management: the OS schedules the disk request, checks permissions, updates buffers
States that both roles run together: abstraction is what the program sees, resource management is what the OS does underneath

bank.q: Describe computer-system organization: CPU, memory, device controllers and buses. Explain how an interrupt lets a device get the CPU's attention.
outline: CPU executes instructions from memory over the system bus; controllers connect devices
Device raises an interrupt request line; CPU finishes current instruction, saves state, jumps via the interrupt vector to a handler
Handler identifies device, does the transfer or sets up DMA, then returns
Contrast polling: the CPU repeatedly checks the device, wasting cycles
Mentions interrupt priorities and masking

bank.q: Explain operating-system operations: dual-mode operation, privileged instructions and the use of a timer. Why are all three needed together?
outline: Mode bit: 0 kernel, 1 user; privileged instructions only in kernel mode
Examples of privileged instructions: set timer, load page-table base, disable interrupts, halt
System call switches to kernel mode; return switches back
Timer decrements and interrupts, so the OS regains the CPU even if user code loops forever
Names the cases that break without them: user code disabling interrupts, overwriting kernel memory, monopolising the CPU

bank.q: List the services an operating system provides and classify them as user-facing services and system-efficiency services.
outline: User-facing: user interface, program execution, I/O operations, file-system manipulation, communication, error detection
System-facing: resource allocation, accounting, protection and security
Gives one concrete example for each service
Notes that some services, such as protection, serve both goals
Mentions system programs as the user-visible layer above these services

bank.q: Define a system call and describe the standard types of system calls with one example from each type.
outline: Definition: programmatic trap into kernel mode on behalf of a user process
Types: process control, file management, device management, information maintenance, communication, protection
Examples: fork/exit, open/read/close, ioctl/read, getpid/time, pipe/send/recv, chmod
Explains the trap mechanism: parameters in registers or on stack, system-call number selects the handler, return value and status
Notes that programmers usually reach them through an API, not directly

bank.q: A user program running in user mode executes a read() call on a file. Trace, step by step, everything that happens from the instruction to the return of data, naming the hardware and OS components involved.
outline: Library wrapper places the system-call number and arguments; executes a trap instruction
CPU switches to kernel mode, saves the program counter and registers, indexes the system-call table
Kernel validates the arguments and the file descriptor, checks permissions
Kernel checks its buffer cache; if missing, issues a disk request and blocks the process, scheduling another
Interrupt from the disk completes the transfer; process is made ready
Data is copied to the user buffer, the process returns to user mode with the byte count

bank.q: Compare monolithic and microkernel structures by placing the scheduler, file system and a graphics driver either in kernel mode or in user mode. Give the performance and reliability consequences of each placement.
outline: Monolithic: all three in kernel mode, direct function calls, fast, but one bug can crash the whole system
Microkernel: scheduler and basic IPC in kernel; file system and driver as user servers, reached by message passing
Reliability gain: a crashed driver can be restarted; smaller trusted code base
Cost: two context switches and message copies per request, so slower
Names hybrid designs (some code in kernel, some outside) and when each choice suits: embedded, real-time, general purpose

bank.q: Explain the separation of policy from mechanism in OS design. Show how a scheduling policy or a login policy can be changed without rewriting the mechanism.
outline: Mechanism: the code that does the work, e.g. the context switch or the list of ready processes
Policy: the decision rule, e.g. priority values, or which users may log in
Example: the kernel provides priorities as a mechanism; a system administrator or loadable module sets the policy
Benefit: the same kernel serves many workloads and sites; fewer privileged-code changes
Mentions table-driven parameters and loadable kernel modules

bank.q: Describe the boot sequence of a personal computer from pressing the power button to a shell prompt, naming the role of firmware, bootloader, kernel and the first user process.
outline: Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) runs from ROM, tests hardware, finds a bootable device
Bootloader (in the boot sector or an EFI partition) loads the kernel image and passes parameters
Kernel initialises memory management, scheduler, drivers; mounts the root file system
Kernel starts the first user process (init/systemd), which starts services
A getty or display manager offers login; the shell runs as a user process issuing system calls
Mentions where a failure shows up (no bootloader, kernel panic, no init)

bank.q: "A microkernel is more reliable but slower than a monolithic kernel." Evaluate this claim, using the cost of inter-process communication and the effect of a faulty device driver.
outline: States the mechanism of the cost: trap, message copy, context switch, reply
Quantifies qualitatively: several switches per request versus one function call; fine for control operations, costly for high-rate I/O
Reliability argument: driver crash isolated, restartable, smaller privileged code
Counter-argument: the kernel still needs correct IPC and memory management, so bugs move rather than vanish; IPC paths become critical code
Concludes with conditions: microkernel wins where availability matters, monolithic where throughput per cycle matters

bank.q: A buggy user program tries to write into a kernel address and then runs an infinite loop. Explain every hardware and OS mechanism that should stop it, and what happens if each one is missing.
outline: Mode bit prevents privileged instructions; without it the program could disable interrupts or load a page table
Address translation and page-table protection bits stop the write and raise a trap; without it kernel memory is corruptible
The trap switches to kernel mode and the OS terminates the process
The timer interrupts the infinite loop and returns control to the scheduler; without it the machine hangs
Protection checks system-call arguments so the program cannot ask the kernel to write on its behalf
States that all mechanisms together, not any one alone, give protection

bank.q: Compare batch, time-sharing and real-time operating systems. Which one suits a railway reservation server and which suits an engine-control unit, and what scheduling goal dominates in each case?
outline: Batch: jobs queued, no interaction, goal is throughput and low idle time
Time-sharing: many interactive users, goal is fast response and fairness
Real-time: goal is meeting deadlines, hard versus soft; predictability beats average speed
Reservation server: time-sharing, response time and fairness across many users
Engine control: real-time, worst-case latency must be bounded; a late answer is a wrong answer
Notes that general-purpose systems can be tuned but cannot guarantee hard deadlines

bank.q: System calls cost time because the CPU changes mode and saves state. Discuss why designers still insist on a controlled entry into the kernel instead of letting programs touch hardware directly, and how the cost can be reduced.
outline: Direct hardware access by any program allows corruption of other processes and of the kernel, and defeats accounting and protection
Controlled entry lets the kernel validate arguments, check permissions and keep a single point of policy
Cost components: mode switch, register save and restore, argument copy, cache effects
Reductions: faster trap instructions, batching, avoiding needless copies with shared memory, vsyscall/vDSO for read-only data like time, fewer but larger calls
Trade-off: too much in user space loses enforcement; too much in kernel loses speed

glossary.def: The part of the operating system that always runs in privileged mode and controls the hardware.
A restricted CPU mode in which application code runs and privileged instructions are refused.
The privileged CPU mode in which the kernel executes all instructions and touches all memory.
A hardware bit that records whether the CPU is currently in kernel mode or user mode.
A deliberate software interrupt used by a program to enter the kernel, as in a system call.
A CPU-detected error or event, such as a page fault or divide by zero, that transfers control to a handler.
Repeatedly reading a device status register to see if it needs attention, instead of waiting for an interrupt.
Hardware that operates a device and exposes registers and buffers to the CPU over a bus.
Kernel code that knows how to program one particular device controller.
A shared set of wires carrying addresses, data and control signals between CPU, memory and controllers.
The fixed set of kernel entry points, called by number, that user programs and libraries use.
A programming interface, such as the POSIX calls, through which a program requests services, often wrapping system calls.
A program that reads user commands and runs them as system programs or system calls.
A program in execution, with its own address space, registers and OS state.
Mechanisms such as pipes and shared memory that let processes exchange data.
An OS design in which each layer uses only the services of the layer below it.
Code that can be added to or removed from a running kernel, commonly used for device drivers.
Programs stored in non-volatile memory that test the hardware and locate a bootloader at power-on.
Tools that combine object files into an executable and place it, with its libraries, into memory to run.
Software that presents virtual hardware on which one or more guest operating systems run.
An isolated group of processes sharing the host kernel, packaged with their own file-system view.
A system whose correctness depends on meeting deadlines as well as producing right answers.
A collection of independent computers that appears to its users as one coherent system.
The amount of work completed per unit time, such as processes finished per second.
